body.text: October 21 marked the first anniversary of Takaichi Sanae’s premiership. One of the defining characteristics of her time in office has been her high approval rating, particularly in comparison with those of her immediate predecessors and even her counterparts abroad. In an era that does not reward incumbents politically, she has managed to maintain a strong connection with public sentiment. The latest polls released in November put her approval rating in the range of 42.8 to 58 percent, with all polls showing a net approval rating in the double digits.

Takaichi’s political opponents have expressed puzzlement at the continued strength of public support for her government. At a press conference, Mizuoka Shunichi, leader of the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan (CDP), remarked that it was “somewhat hard to believe that she enjoys such a level of public confidence that her approval rating shows no signs of declining.” He went on to say that he struggled to understand why the Takaichi Cabinet continued to enjoy such high approval ratings, given that some members of the public remained skeptical of her policies and the government’s handling of key issues.

While Mizuoka’s comments reflect the difficulties facing left-wing parties in the current political climate, his observation also points to a prescient distinction between public approval of Takaichi as a political leader and support for her actual policies. Indeed, several of her signature policy initiatives, including revisions to the Imperial House Law and a proposed consumption tax cut, have generated considerable controversy.

The former, in particular, drew criticism from across the editorial spectrum, with all four major national newspapers – Yomiuri, Asahi, Mainichi, and Nikkei – opposing the proposed changes. Their editorials raised concerns ranging from the potential destabilization of the imperial succession and the exclusion of female-line succession to constitutional questions and the lack of sufficient cross-party consensus. Notably, Takaichi’s approval rating experienced a marked decline around the time the legislation was passed.

The consumption tax cut bill, which would temporarily reduce the tax rate on food products from 8 to 1 percent for a two-year period, has also provoked a backlash among traditional conservatives within the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). They regard the consumption tax as an important source of revenue for social security and prioritize fiscal discipline to contain the cost of servicing Japan’s enormous public debt. When the bill passed the Lower House, four LDP members, including former Prime Minister Ishiba Shigeru, abstained from voting, prompting the party leadership to reprimand them.

However, while the public has remained uncertain or lukewarm toward certain aspects of Takaichi’s policies, it has shown strong support for others that might have sparked considerably more controversy in the past. Alongside the consumption tax cut bill, another major piece of legislation being deliberated this fall would reduce the number of Diet members elected through the proportional representation system by 31 seats, equivalent to approximately 7 percent of the total membership of the Diet. Opinion polls have shown in the past six months that nearly 60 to 70 percent of the public support this initiative.

On defense policy, too, the Takaichi administration’s efforts to overturn or substantially revise long-standing principles have encountered relatively little public backlash. In April, the administration greenlighted Japanese companies to export arms, including lethal weapons, even to destinations that could be active conflict zones, provided that such exports were deemed to serve Japan’s national interests.

Furthermore, reports suggest that the forthcoming national security documents may include an exception to Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles, allowing the introduction of American nuclear weapons onto Japanese soil. Such a move would effectively institutionalize remarks made by Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya in 2010, in which he suggested that nuclear weapons deployment could be considered under the most extreme circumstances. If formally incorporated into government policy, this change would effectively mark the end of another longstanding pillar of Japanese defense policy, once regarded as virtually sacrosanct.

While the public may not agree with all of her policies, it seems willing to reward Takaichi for her willingness to challenge conventional wisdom. For the broader public, her combative stance toward the technocrats and experts who have long guided Japan’s fiscal policy – and who are often associated with decades of economic stagnation – offers a departure from the status quo and a glimpse of hope for revitalizing the Japanese economy.

For conservatives, meanwhile, Takaichi has provided long-awaited red meat by pursuing controversial policies that they have advocated for years but were previously unable to realize under the constraints of political pragmatism. And while Takaichi has so far governed pragmatically, her decision to pay her respects in the direction of Yasukuni Shrine from Nippon Budokan (about ten minutes away) sent a signal that she has not forgotten her conservative base and intends to govern as a conservative to the extent permitted by the realities of holding office.

Although it is true that Takaichi’s approval rating has declined since her inauguration, what has made the political environment even more favorable for her is the lack of any significant opposition within the Diet. Left-wing opposition parties have been largely marginalized or weakened by Takaichi’s landslide victory in the February election. Meanwhile, centrist parties appear increasingly willing to support the government’s legislative agenda, allowing them to avoid direct confrontation with the administration while the next national elections remain some way off.

Takaichi remains popular with the public despite the unpopularity of some of her policies because voters are rewarding her prioritization of action over than the status quo. This is the cardinal truth that explains Takaichi’s political success so far – and one that the opposition could emulate to rise from the ashes. However, thus far the opposition continues to struggle to understand that magic.
